title: Why Do Freight Trains Have Engines in the Middle?
description:
Some freight trains in North America are longer than three kilometers, almost two miles of steel boxes. And if you watch one pass, something strange happens. Halfway through, there is another locomotive. Sometimes there is one at the very end too, pushing. No crew inside. It is being driven by radio from the front. Today, ten parts of a giant freight train, and why each one exists.

Machine Reverse takes apart the machines you see every day and explains, part by part, why each one exists. This video covers 10 parts.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
1:17 1. The engine in the middle
2:44 2. The slack between cars
4:09 3. The weak link
5:32 4. The box at the end
6:49 5. The caboose
8:14 6. The grids on the roof
9:41 7. The double stack
10:59 8. The hill in the yard
12:14 9. The loop
13:39 10. The triangle of lights
15:02 The verdict

Sources:
- Distributed power (radio-controlled remote locomotives, Locotrol): Wikipedia, "Distributed power" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_power
- Slack action and draft gear: Wikipedia, "Slack action" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slack_action and "Draft gear" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draft_gear
- Knuckle couplers and spare knuckles: Wikipedia, "Railway coupling" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_coupling
- End-of-train devices and two-way EOT rules: US FRA, 49 CFR Part 232 Subpart E https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-II/part-232/subpart-E and Wikipedia, "End-of-train device" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End-of-train_device
- Caboose and its disappearance in the 1980s: Wikipedia, "Caboose" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caboose
- Dynamic braking and resistor grids: Wikipedia, "Dynamic braking" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_braking
- Double-stack rail transport and tunnel clearance projects: Wikipedia, "Double-stack rail transport" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-stack_rail_transport
- Hump yards and car retarders: Wikipedia, "Classification yard" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classification_yard and "Car retarder" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Car_retarder
- Tehachapi Loop (1876): Wikipedia, "Tehachapi Loop" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tehachapi_Loop
- Ditch lights (auxiliary alerting lights): US FRA, 49 CFR 229.125 https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-II/part-229/subpart-C/subject-group-ECFRe3e3b49e4e5c9b4/section-229.125
- Train stopping distances at crossings: Operation Lifesaver, "Train facts" https://oli.org/
